extracted.intended_audience: jurors, judges, and attorneys in U.S. patent infringement trials (jury instruction template)
extracted.subtask_description: A model set of jury instructions describing legal standards for patent infringement (including inducement, contributory, means-plus-function, doctrine of equivalents, 35 U.S.C. §271 variants) and for invalidity defenses (prior art, anticipation, public use, on-sale bar, etc.). Designed to be adapted with case-specific facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful blindness (inducement knowledge standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find willful blindness: (1) [the Defendant] must have subjectively believed that there was a high probability that a patent existed covering [the accused product/process] and (2) [the Defendant] must have taken deliberate actions to avoid learning of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-prong subjective standard drawn from Global-Tech: high probability belief plus deliberate avoidance of confirming information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induced infringement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To find that [the Defendant] induced infringement, it is not necessary to show that [the Defendant] has directly infringed as long as you find that someone has directly infringed. However, if there is no direct infringement by anyone, [the Defendant] cannot have induced infringement of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on 35 U.S.C. § 271(b) and cases such as Global‑Tech and Grokster; induced infringement requires a direct infringer—absence of any direct infringement precludes inducement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement (elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish contributory infringement, [the Plaintiff] must prove that it is more likely than not that [the Defendant] had knowledge of the patent, and that: (1) someone other than [the Defendant] has directly infringed the patent; (2) [the Defendant] sold, offered for sale, or imported within the United States a component of the infringing product or an apparatus for use in the infringing process; (3) the component or apparatus is not a staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use; (4) the component or apparatus constitutes a material part of the patented invention; and (5) [the Defendant] knew that the component was especially made or adapted for use in an infringing product/method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of the patent is required; not necessary that defendant directly infringed so long as someone else directly infringed. Cites 35 U.S.C. § 271(c) and relevant Federal Circuit authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use' is something that has uses other than as a part or component of the patented product (or other than in the patented method), and those other uses are not occasional, farfetched, impractical, experimental, or hypothetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in assessing element (3) of contributory infringement; courts focus on whether noninfringing uses are substantial and real, not merely theoretical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement of means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. §112) — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims containing means-plus-function or step-plus-function clauses, [the Plaintiff] must prove that it is more likely than not that the part/step of the Defendant's product/method that performs the claimed function is identical to, or equivalent to, the structure/step described in the specification for performing the identical function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First determine whether the accused product/method has any structure/step that performs the claimed function; if none exists, the means-plus-function limitation is not infringed. If it does, identify the accused structure/act and compare it to the structure/acts disclosed in the specification for identity or equivalence (person of ordinary skill perspective). Cites 35 U.S.C. §112 and Federal Circuit precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function infringement — Alternative identification and comparison procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative I: If the accused product/method performs the claimed function, identify the structure/step in the accused product that performs it and determine whether that structure/step is identical to, or equivalent to, any structure/step identified in the patent specification as performing the function. Alternative II: Identify the structure/act in the accused product that performs the function and determine whether that structure/act is identical to, or equivalent to, the specific corresponding structure/acts the court identified during claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the court-identified corresponding structure (if court has done claim construction) in comparing for equivalence. Equivalence is judged from perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art; insubstantial differences indicate equivalence. If all claim requirements are met by structures found in the accused product, the accused product infringes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence standard for means-plus-function (person of ordinary skill test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the structure/act of the accused product is equivalent to a structure/act described in the patent specification is decided from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art. If a person of ordinary skill in the art would consider the differences between the structure/act found in the Defendant's product and a structure/act described in the patent specification to be insubstantial, the structures/acts are equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess insubstantiality of differences; apply Federal Circuit precedent listed (e.g., Cybor, In re Donaldson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of dependent claims (literal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim refers to at least one other claim and incorporates all elements of the claim to which it refers plus additional elements. To establish literal infringement of a dependent claim, [the Plaintiff] must show that it is more likely than not that the Defendant's product/method includes each and every element of the dependent claim. If the independent claim from which the dependent claim depends is not literally infringed, then the dependent claim cannot be literally infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify differences between the independent and dependent claims; dependent claim requires all elements of the independent claim plus its own additional elements. Citations to Federal Circuit cases provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of 'comprising' (open-ended) claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'comprising' means 'including the following but not excluding others.' If the Defendant's product/method includes all elements in the claim, the fact that it includes additional components or steps does not avoid literal infringement of a claim that uses 'comprising' language so long as the additional components/steps do not negate an element of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether extra components negate an element; if not, comprising claims remain infringed despite additional features. Cases cited (Invitrogen, AFG, Moleculon, AB Dick).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. §271(f)(1) — supplying substantial portion of components abroad (elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under Section 271(f)(1), Plaintiff must prove it is more likely than not that (1) the product as intended to be assembled outside the U.S. included all limitations of at least one asserted claim, (2) Defendant supplied or caused to be supplied components from the U.S. that made up all or a substantial portion of the invention of any one asserted claim, and (3) Defendant specifically intended to induce the combination of the components into a product that would infringe the patent if assembled in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires intent to induce combination and that components supplied from the U.S. made up all or a substantial portion; cites Cardiac Pacemakers, Microsoft v. AT&T, and other authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. §271(f)(2) — supplying components especially made or adapted for use abroad (elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under Section 271(f)(2), Plaintiff must prove it is more likely than not that (1) Defendant actually supplied components from the U.S. to a foreign country or caused them to be supplied, (2) Defendant knew or should have known that the components were especially made or adapted for use in a product that infringes the patent, (3) those components have no substantial non-infringing use, and (4) Defendant intended for the components to be combined into that product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that the components actually were combined into an infringing product, so long as Defendant intended they be combined into a product that would have infringed if combined in the U.S. Cases cited include Cardiac Pacemakers, Microsoft v. AT&T, Waymark, Rotec.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. §271(g) — infringement by import/sale/use of product made by patented process (elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under Section 271(g), Plaintiff must prove it is more likely than not that (1) Defendant imported/sold/offered for sale/used a product that was made by a process including all steps of at least one asserted claim, (2) the product was made between the patent issue date and expiration (or date of trial), and (3) Defendant imported/sold/offered/used the product between the patent issue date and expiration (or date of trial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must decide whether evidence establishes the product was 'made by' the patented process. Exclude if the product was materially changed by later processes or the product is only a trivial/non-essential part of another product. Note on Section 295 presumption where patentee cannot determine the process (may require accused infringer to rebut presumption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents — element-by-element equivalence analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Defendant's product/method does not literally infringe an asserted claim, the jury must decide whether it infringes under the doctrine of equivalents. Under this doctrine, the product/method can infringe if it includes parts/steps that are equivalent to claim requirements that are not literally present. If the product/method is missing an equivalent part/step to even one claim part/step, it cannot infringe under the doctrine of equivalents; the analysis must be done for each individual requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence is determined such that a part/step is equivalent if a person of ordinary skill would think the differences are not substantial as of the time of alleged infringement. One way is the function-way-result (FWR) test: performed substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result. Known interchangeability may be considered but is not necessary. The same accused element may satisfy more than one claim element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on doctrine of equivalents — prior art (ensnarement)
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not find that the Defendant's product/method infringes under the doctrine of equivalents if by doing so the patent claim would cover products/methods that were already in the prior art. Defendant has the burden of coming forward with evidence to show that it was in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensnarement is ultimately a question of law for the court, but the jury may be asked for an advisory verdict in some cases. Cases cited (DePuy Spine, Fiskars, Conroy, Wilson Sporting Goods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on doctrine of equivalents — prosecution history estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: If the court has determined that prosecution history estoppel applies to certain claim elements (i.e., an amendment was made for reasons related to patentability and presumption of surrender of equivalents has not been rebutted), the doctrine of equivalents analysis cannot be applied to those claim elements. Those elements must be literally present in the Defendant's product/method for there to be infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The instruction assumes the court has made an estoppel determination as a matter of law; list of estopped elements should be provided claim-by-claim. Cites Festo and Warner-Jenkinson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on doctrine of equivalents — subject matter dedicated to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent discloses subject matter but does not include it within its claims, the patentee has dedicated that unclaimed subject matter to the public. If the patent discloses but does not claim subject matter alleged to be equivalent to an element, then that component/step alleged to be equivalent in Defendant's product/method cannot be an equivalent for purposes of the doctrine of equivalents, even if the failure to claim was unintentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court should list elements that were disclosed but unclaimed; unless each such element is literally present there can be no infringement under the doctrine of equivalents for those elements. Cases cited include Pfizer and Toro.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of invalidity defense (burden and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that the asserted claim(s) of the patents-in-suit are invalid. [The Defendant] must prove that it is highly probable that each asserted claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury must determine whether each asserted claim is invalid. The instruction introduces more detailed invalidity contentions to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art defined (categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes any of the following items received into evidence during trial: (1) any product/method publicly known or used by others in the United States before the patented invention was made; (2) patents that issued more than one year before the filing date of the patent, or before the invention was made; (3) publications dated more than one year before the filing date of the patent, or before the invention was made; (4) any product/method in public use or on sale in the U.S. more than one year before the patent was filed; (5) any product/method made by anyone before the named inventors created the patented product/method where the product/method was not abandoned, suppressed, or concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list is illustrative and the court may add additional types of prior art. Citation: 35 U.S.C. § 102.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art considered or not considered by the USPTO (weighting)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party challenging validity relies on prior art that was considered by the Examiner during prosecution, that party's ability to satisfy its 'highly probable' evidence burden may be more difficult. When a party presents evidence that was not considered by the Examiner, such new evidence may be given more weight and may make it easier to satisfy the burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance based on Microsoft v. i4i and Federal Circuit precedent: evidence not previously considered by the Examiner can be particularly persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity of independent and dependent claims (evaluation rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: You must evaluate the invalidity of each asserted claim separately. If you find that a dependent claim is invalid, then you cannot find that the independent claim to which that dependent claim refers is not invalid. Conversely, an independent claim can be found invalid, even though a dependent claim to which it refers is valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims incorporate all elements of the claims they refer to plus additional elements; apply case law (Comparer, Callaway, Ormco) when assessing interdependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) — perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of invalidity of a patent claim is determined from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in the field of the asserted invention as of [date].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: POSITA perspective is used throughout validity analyses (anticipation, obviousness, inherency, understandings of disclosures). Court should set the appropriate date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (novelty) — single-reference rule and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove anticipation, Defendant must prove it is highly probable that the claimed invention is not new. To anticipate a claim, each and every element in the claim must be present in a single item of prior art, and arranged or combined in the same way as recited in the claim. You may not combine two or more items of prior art to find anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider what a person of ordinary skill would have understood from review of the reference. Optional inherency instruction: consider not only what is expressly disclosed but also what is inherently present or results from practicing the prior art; inherency requires high probability and may be shown with evidence outside the reference (including testing). Cite Net MoneyIN, Toro, Schering, In re Robertson, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public knowledge (anticipation by public knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the invention defined in that claim was publicly known by others in the United States before it was invented by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is a factual issue about date of invention, the jury should be instructed how to determine invention date; otherwise the court may instruct the date of invention as appropriate. Cite 35 U.S.C. §102(a) and cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public use (public use bar)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if more than one year before the filing date an embodiment of the claimed invention was both (1) accessible to the public or commercially exploited in the United States; and (2) ready for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention is in public use if it was accessible to the public or commercially exploited. Relevant factors: nature of public activity, public access, confidentiality obligations, commercial exploitation, circumstances of testing and experimentation. Secret use by a third party is not public unless public or employees had access. 'Ready for patenting' means reduced to practice or drawings/descriptions sufficient for a POSITA to make/use. Cite 35 U.S.C. §102(a),(b) and cases (Clock Spring, Invitrogen, SmithKline, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar (35 U.S.C. §102(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if more than one year before filing an embodiment of the claimed invention was (1) subject to a commercial offer for sale in the United States and (2) ready for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commercial 'offer for sale' exists if another party could make a binding contract by accepting the offer; embodiment need not have been actually sold. Essential question: whether there was an attempt to obtain commercial benefit. Conceived date and 'ready for patenting' definitions (reduced to practice or sufficient description) apply. Cite Pfaff v. Wells, August Tech, Atlanta Attachment, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception to public use / on-sale
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain activities are experimental if they are a legitimate effort to test claimed features or to determine if the invention will work for its intended purpose. So long as the primary purpose is experimentation, it does not matter that the public used the invention or that the inventor incidentally derived profit from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only experimentation by or under control of the inventor or assignee qualifies for the exception; experimentation by a third party for its own purposes generally does not qualify. The court must evaluate the primary purpose and control of testing to determine if an asserted public use/sale was experimental.
